questions.why: Use the adverb 'well' to describe how she sings, not the adjective 'good'.
After linking verbs like 'taste', use an adjective: 'good', not 'well'.

questions.q: He worked ___ all weekend to finish the report.
questions.why: 'Hard' is both adjective and adverb; 'hardly' means 'almost not'.
'Hardly' means 'almost not', so it fits 'know almost nothing'.
Adverbs of manner usually end in '-ly' and describe the verb 'drives'.
Adverbs of frequency like 'never' go before the main verb but after 'be'.

questions.q: I ___ go to the gym before work.
questions.why: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: 'usually go'.
With perfect tenses, the frequency adverb goes between 'have' and the past participle.
Adjective order is size, then age, then colour: big (size), old (age), red (colour).
Opinion comes first, then colour, then material: nice, black, leather.
Order is opinion, age, then origin: beautiful, ancient, Chinese.
With multiple adverbials the natural order is manner, place, time: 'angrily in the office yesterday'.
Place usually comes before time/manner in this case: 'at the station late'.

questions.q: It was ___ a boring film that I fell asleep.
questions.why: Use 'such' before a noun phrase (a + adjective + noun); 'so' goes before an adjective alone.
Use 'so' before an adjective with no noun: 'so difficult'.

questions.q: This coffee is ___ hot to drink.
questions.why: 'Too' before an adjective means 'more than acceptable': too hot.

questions.q: He isn't ___ to reach the shelf.
questions.why: 'Enough' comes after the adjective: 'tall enough'.

questions.q: She is ___ student that everyone admires her.
questions.why: With a singular countable noun use 'such a + adjective + noun'.

questions.q: I have ___ time to finish this.
questions.why: Before a noun, 'enough' means a sufficient amount: 'enough time'.
Use the adverb 'well' to describe how they behaved.
Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: 'always arrives'.
'Such' is used before 'a + adjective + noun': such a wonderful time.

questions.q: This box is ___ heavy for me to lift.
questions.why: 'Too + adjective' shows excess preventing an action.
Use the '-ly' adverb to describe how she speaks.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'He plays the piano very ___ (good).'
questions.why: The adverb of 'good' is 'well' when describing how someone does something.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'I ___ (frequency: never) eat breakfast before 9.' Use the frequency adverb before the verb.
questions.why: 'Never' is placed before the main verb to show zero frequency.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'It was ___ a long day that we all went to bed early.'
questions.why: Use 'such' before 'a + adjective + noun'.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'The water was ___ cold to swim in.' (excess)
questions.why: 'Too + adjective' expresses excess that prevents the action.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'She isn't old ___ to drive.' (sufficiency, after adjective)
questions.why: 'Enough' follows the adjective: 'old enough'.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'Put the adjectives in order: a ___ ___ ___ table (round / wooden / small).'
questions.why: Order is size, shape, then material: small, round, wooden.
Frequency adverbs go after the verb 'be'.
An adverb ('fluently') modifies the verb 'speaks'.

questions.q: I ___ go to the gym on Fridays.
questions.why: Frequency adverb before the main verb: 'I usually go'.
'Taste' is a linking verb, so it takes an adjective, not an adverb.
'Almost' goes between the auxiliary and the main verb.
